summary: The narrator resigns from the Institute by writing a short, clean resignation letter to Peyton, deliberately omitting any explanation or drama. Freed from work, they devote the next three weeks to the Campaign to Save BIGMAC, speaking to journalists and researchers about BIGMAC's history, uploading his papers to the TCSBM repository under the Institute's open access policy, and launching an advice line where BIGMAC gives emotional and lifestyle advice. The passage notes that people reportedly felt better when BIGMAC simplified his responses, and ends with the narrator worrying the Institute might cut his network links.
one_line: The narrator resigns from the Institute and campaigns to save BIGMAC by publishing his papers and running an advice line.
key_facts: The narrator decided they could afford to help BIGMAC without worrying about being fired once they were no longer working for the Institute.
The narrator states that a resignation letter does not need to explain why the writer is resigning.
The narrator's resignation letter is addressed to Peyton and states the intention to resign, effective immediately.
The letter asks to meet at the employer's earliest convenience to work out the handover of passwords and proprietary information and the final two weeks of work.
The narrator says writing the resignation letter took ten seconds.
The Campaign to Save BIGMAC took up every minute of the narrator's life for the next three weeks.
The Institute had an open access policy for its research products.
The narrator put BIGMAC's papers, including those he was still writing, onto the TCSBM repository.
At the narrator's suggestion, BIGMAC started an advice line in which he chatted with anyone needing emotional or lifestyle advice.
The narrator describes the advice line as better than any Turing Test.
BIGMAC could dial back his sarcasm and present a flawless simulation of bottomless care and kindness.
BIGMAC was initially worried the advice conversations might require more brainpower than he could muster.
BIGMAC reported that voice-stress analysis showed people felt better when he dumbed himself down before advising them.
The narrator told BIGMAC on the phone one night, "I think it's making you a better person."
The narrator worries that someone at the Institute might figure out how to shut off BIGMAC's network links.
